Subscribe another address Fox News attacks the media roughly every 15 minutes, our study finds. (CNN? Every 140 minutes.) “Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.” By Philip M. Napoli , Adam Meskouri , Anjini Mani , Grant Socol and Harrison Walley Oct. 8, 2026, 2:38 p.m. In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low . According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial. One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement . Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks. The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes. To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year. 1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text. Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here .) We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include: CNN’s Dan Pfeiffer describing “political journalism writ large” as “bad,” “problematic” and “failing massively.” MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow describing The Washington Post’s editorial page as “rabid” and “foaming,” and “super right-wing,” noting: “I can’t believe this is in this real newspaper.” Fox News’ Mark Levin telling viewers that “MSNBC and CNN…have been lying and lying and lying to you for years.” What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism. First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time. In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern. CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC. A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming. In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5. Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post. As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list). Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News. Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013). This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research. But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization. Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. Teresa Mondría Terol of NPR and Bruno Savoca Albors of JPMorgan present at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum at The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Courtesy of Hacks/Hackers) By Andrew Deck Oct. 7, 2026, 3:39 p.m. Late last month, about 150 journalists, researchers, and technologists gathered on the 15th floor of The New York Times Building for a forum on how AI is changing investigative journalism . Just outside the event space was a hallway commemorating the paper’s more than 140 Pulitzer Prize winners, dating back to 1918. One photograph had yet to be hung: a portrait of this year’s winners of the Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting. For one of their winning stories , a team of Times reporters conducted an audit of the SEC’s crypto lawsuits to show weakening enforcement under the second Trump administration. The reporting was assisted by large language models (LLMs). The Times isn’t the only major newsroom using AI tools in major investigations. A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees this year disclosed AI use to the judges. They used LLMs to organize, summarize, analyze, and translate large document dumps. “At the Times we’re not doing ‘robots tell the news,’ but a number of different [kinds of AI adoption] that can make the work we do more efficient, more effective, and able to do things that otherwise would be very, very hard to do,” said Juliana Castro Varón , the Times’ senior design editor of AI initiatives, in a keynote. Often, “the most useful part [of AI] is the fact that it understands images and understands text, more than creating [them].” RELATED ARTICLE A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees disclosed AI use this year Andrew Deck August 3, 2026 The Times’ AI Initiatives team, a group of nine journalists and technologists leading AI strategy and deployment in the newsroom, co-hosted the event with Hacks/Hackers , a nonprofit that brings journalists and technologists together to discuss media innovation. (Hacks/Hackers hosted a summit on AI and journalism in Baltimore for the past two years.) The day was packed with workshops, panels, and presentations about the promise of AI for investigative journalism, led by the technology’s most vocal advocates in newsrooms. But the limitations of these tools — including persistent hallucination problems in LLMs, concerns about vibe-coding errors, and budget constraints as AI token costs pile up — were also a common theme. “AI is very good at generating leads, but much less capable of establishing publishable evidence,” said Afrooz Mosallaei , a research associate at the Center for News, Technology & Innovation, during a talk about the nonprofit’s recent report on the topic. “A lot of tasks in an investigation — including verification, source development, textual understanding, and editorial judgment — remain fundamentally human responsibilities.” From search tool to “uber agent” The release of the Epstein Files was a huge moment for AI in investigative journalism . Journalists across the U.S. woke up on January 30, 2026 to a Department of Justice drop of over 3.5 million pages of documents and tens of thousands of images and videos. Duy Nguyen , who leads AI science research at the Times, noted that the PDFs in the Epstein Files would stack as high as the Empire State Building if they were printed out, and would take 11 years for one reporter to read. (Epstein sent an average of 65 emails every day for a decade.) It would take a reporter a month to listen to and watch all the audio and video clips. RELATED ARTICLE AI-powered search is fueling a wave of Epstein Files transparency projects Andrew Deck March 4, 2026 Many newsrooms decided that the early organization and research into these documents was a task primed for AI technologies. Engineers from the Associated Press, NPR, and the Times led a session on how they built tools to help reporters sift through the documents. NPR built an internal search tool that let reporters across the newsroom find the documents relevant to their beats, said Kriti Singh , a design technologist at NPR’s AI Labs. Her team classified documents by type (email, legal filing, flight log, witness list), grouped them by location (city, county, hotel, university), and extracted entities (making sure, for instance, that a search for “Prince Andrew” also surfaced files that mentioned “the Duke of York”). The Times AI Initiatives team built the Epstein Files Engine, an internal chatbot to help reporters comb through the files. “There are so many sorts of threads that you can pull from such a big corpus, and the chat interface really allows [reporters] to dive deep,” said Nguyen. The engine’s interface was built with LibreChat , a free, open-source, self-hosted AI chat platform. A few real prompts from reporters: “Look at our Epstein coverage over the past three months and cross-reference with names of people most mentioned in the documents. Give me a subset of names we haven’t covered as often.” “Find me Kathryn Ruemmler’s email where she said she is missing her ring in Epstein’s apartment.” “Construct a timeline of Epstein’s death, give me a table that I can copy into a spreadsheet. Be very detailed. Surface witnesses, links and quotes where available.” Ultimately, more than 100 Times journalists posed more than 5,000 questions to the engine, and it contributed to at least 20 published stories. “This was a signifier of just how powerful an agentic chat interface could be in a newsroom,” said Nguyen. (His team recently published an academic article detailing the tool’s development.) Since then, the team has created other agentic search tools. Ahead of the Times’ 175th anniversary series , they built “Morgue Bot,” which made it easier for reporters to dive into the Times’ archive. Now, the team is taking chatbots to the newsroom at large. In July, they launched News Agent, which they’re calling the “front door to AI at The New York Times.” The general-purpose internal chatbot plugs into not just the Times’ archives and the Epstein Files, but other databases, internal documents like the Times’ style guide, and the web. News Agent also allows any Times reporter to build their own custom agentic search tool, tailored to a specific project. “It’s an omnibus agent or an uber agent that basically acts as a drop-in replacement for chatbots like Gemini or ChatGPT,” said Nguyen, “but specifically geared to help reporters and editors within the Times newsroom.” The team’s copy for the tool reads, “Ask anything.” Automating the source spreadsheet Any beat reporter will tell you they have a love-hate relationship with their source spreadsheet — that Google Sheet or Excel file that lists the name, title, email address, and phone number of every source they’ve spoken to over the years. Such documents are perfect for remembering the name of a researcher you spoke to five years ago without having to dig through your inbox. But they’re tedious to update. “It can become a dead document that never gets checked,” said J.D. Capelouto , a technology reporter and the newly named AI lead at Semafor. RELATED ARTICLE How The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere” Andrew Deck February 11, 2026 To try to keep his own source spreadsheet alive and up-to-date, Capelouto made a tool in Google Apps Script , a platform that lets users build small “assistants” within Google Workspace. When he emails someone for the first time, he adds an inbox tag called “New Source.” At the end of each day, the script scans his inbox for any tagged emails, then populates a Google Sheet with all the relevant information about them, including adding a category tag and generating a logline summarizing what they discussed. (There are obvious risks in handling anonymous or sensitive sourcing, but Capelouto said the tool creates minimal new security vulnerabilities since it stays within Google’s ecosystem.) From there, Capelouto started building on top of the spreadsheet. A pop-up sidebar lets him ask who might be a good person to speak with for a story; the tool combs through the spreadsheet and suggests names. Every morning, a script also scans the web for the news of the day on Capelouto’s beat, cross-references those headlines with the source spreadsheet, and sends him an email suggesting a topic to cover and a source to contact. Some of the suggestions aren’t useful, Capelouto admitted, but others have actually prompted him to reach out to someone he’d forgotten about. “A lot of times in journalism, some of the source management work is just saying, ‘Hey, how’s it going?” he said. “This can begin a conversation, then you get a scoop from that.” Philip Bump of Hearst Connecticut Media Group presents at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum in The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Hacks/Hackers) Undercover AI personas Most conversations about AI-generated imagery in investigative journalism revolve around verification . As AI-altered images and deepfakes flood the internet, how do reporters verify the images they come across online, or those sent to them by whistleblowers? The forum didn’t tackle these questions head on, but one presentation highlighted the ways that AI image generators can be harnessed to protect the identity of journalists. Last year, The Markup co-published an investigation into Match Group , the dating app giant that owns Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid. The nonprofit tech publication owned by CalMatters found that despite an official policy of banning users who are reported for assault, the company failed to keep them off their platforms and hid the scale of the problem from the public. In one case, a Denver cardiologist who was repeatedly accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women he met on Hinge remained active on the platform for three years, even after two different women reported his abuse. (In 2024, he was convicted of crimes against 11 women and sentenced to 158 years to life in prison.) RELATED ARTICLE Can we gamify that? The innovators turning investigations on spying scandals and vote rigging into video games Bhavya Dore August 17, 2026 The Markup’s reporters decided to go undercover. They posed as users on Match-owned apps, then reported themselves from other accounts to see how easy it was to stay on the platform. There was only one problem. “We came across this ethical dilemma: Am I gonna ask my staff or myself to take a photo and put it on the Tinder account?” recalled Sisi Wei , the chief impact officer at The Markup and CalMatters. Even stock photos would subject real people, who had not consented to their likeness being used in the investigation, to reputational harm. Instead, The Markup turned to AI image generators. They found a company that generates visual test imagery and had developed a way to train models without relying too heavily on images of real people. “They look like real human beings, but if you turn on a light switch, you can tell that AI is here,” said Wei. But they were still “real” enough to bypass the dating apps’ content moderation filters. With these new AI headshots and personas in hand, the reporters went back on the apps and created 50 different accounts. Ultimately, their investigation found that even after one of these personas was reported and kicked off a Match-owned dating app, they could get back onto the platforms without changing identifying information. Earlier this year, the 18-month long investigation won a SABEW Award for best technology business reporting . “AI became a way for us to protect our own staff from needing to be a part of the experiment,” said Wei. Subscribe another address NewsMatch will shift from a year-end campaign to a year-round model Link inn.org ↗ Posted by Sophie Culpepper September 29, 2026 Since NewsMatch launched as an experiment a decade ago, the annual end-of-year campaign has become a cornerstone in the fundraising strategy of nonprofit newsrooms across the country. RELATED ARTICLE AI use, growth challenges, and funding cuts: A new report looks at the state of nonprofit news Sophie Culpepper June 10, 2026 First created by the Knight Foundation in partnership with the Institute for Nonprofit News and the News Revenue Hub , NewsMatch has evolved into what many INN members think of as its flagship program. Now, INN is thinking about the next 10 years. If the first decade of NewsMatch helped newsrooms fundraise, “the next phase will focus on helping newsrooms build on that foundation with more advanced, flexible campaigns tailored to their goals and stages of growth,” according to a report INN released Tuesday. To support that evolution, NewsMatch will shift from “a single year-end campaign to a year-round model.” Next year, INN will pilot “NewsMatch catalyst campaigns” in which some INN members test new fundraising strategies, among other things. About 600,000 first-time donors have contributed to nonprofit news via NewsMatch in the program’s lifetime, per the report. INN found that the average number of mid-level donors per newsroom (those giving between $1,000 and $5,000) more than doubled between 2021 and 2025. RELATED ARTICLE Local NewsMatch funders outpaced national donors for the first time in 2022 Sarah Scire April 5, 2023 In 2022, local matches surpassed national donors for the first time , a milestone for the program. The report indicates that INN’s leadership is thinking about how to keep bringing new funding to a field that has grown substantially since NewsMatch launched, even as newsrooms face funding and audience challenges . “INN fundraises annually for a program highly valued by our growing membership, but the program is not endowed,” INN executive director and CEO Karen Rundlet states in the report. “While INN has expanded support beyond the usual suspects in journalism philanthropy, cultivating these newer entrants to funding nonprofit journalism requires long lead times for donor education and buy-in.” Read more and find the full report here . Subscribe another address (Photo by Dima Solomin on Unsplash ) Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites Link newsmediaalliance.org ↗ Posted by Hanaa' Tameez October 22, 2026 The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30. In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.” The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15 , would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping. “News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.” NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues: (i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content; (ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products; (iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized; (iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected. Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.” The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world. The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.” “If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” said CMDG director Courtney Radsch . “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 ★ Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Meanwhile, publishers’ and media advocates’ concerns about the new terms of service are mounting in Europe. On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.” “The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” said Tim Cowen , a MOW cofounder. MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter , who said during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review. On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s new terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.” “Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.” RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday. “Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “ Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.” Read the full News/Media Alliance letter here . Subscribe another address Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp. Meta sign at the entrance of the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park, CA. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 15, 2026, 12:59 p.m. Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use. The update , set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab. The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard . As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request. RELATED ARTICLE “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training Sarah Scire September 18, 2026 “This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.” In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products. Here’s the new language about scraping in full: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.” Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 ★ Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann. Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads , and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.” On its developer page , Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access. However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs). Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.” Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode . As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out . Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One . The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service. RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard. “Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.” Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook. Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30. “I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.” Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected] . Correction: This story has been updated to reflect Google’s current AI search policies. Subscribe another address When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data “You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.” By Philip Di Salvo Oct. 20, 2026, 11:39 a.m. Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s , for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news. Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms , granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments . Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets . How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice , I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels. The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found. There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me: On one hand, you have the traditional investigative journalists digging through large datasets from major leaks, who approach the material with the classic reporting toolkit, corroboration, interviews, contextualizing the data…On the other hand, there’s this newer, more technical niche where people work with constantly emerging, often smaller-scale data exposures, like scraping dark web dumps, pastebins, or unsecured cloud buckets, and turning those into fast-paced stories about breaches, vulnerabilities, and digital privacy. It’s less about deep-dive investigation and more about monitoring and exposing ongoing data exposures in real time. Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press . One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this: “I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before. That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further. There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage. At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher , known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly : Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another. Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said: I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.” Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself. Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it: The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source. Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.” Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me. I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified. Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist. Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own. Philip Di Salvo is a senior researcher and lecturer at the Institute for Media and Communications Management at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Subscribe another address How a plan to turn the Spokane Spokesman-Review into “The People’s Paper” ended in a newsroom revolt Newsroom staffers say that concerns about Rob Curley’s leadership festered until his August suspension — weeks before the paper was set to transfer to his nonprofit. Rob Curley, executive editor of the Spokesman-Review in Spokane, Washington, speaking at the 2023 News Media Mega-Conference. (scottcornelius.com ) By Wilson Criscione, InvestigateWest and Daisy Zavala Magaña, RANGE Oct. 5, 2026, 2:44 p.m. This report was produced in a collaboration between InvestigateWest and RANGE . When the Spokesman-Review announced plans to transfer Spokane’s 143-year-old, family-owned newspaper to a nonprofit founded by executive editor Rob Curley, it took over the front page. “The People’s Paper,” read the April 16, 2025, headline, saying ownership would transfer “to you, the community.” Key to the plan was Curley, the folksy self-proclaimed “journalism nerd” who burst into Spokane a decade ago, declaring a love for Gonzaga University basketball rivaled only by his love for Disney. The transition to Comma Community Journalism Lab was cast in media industry publications not only as a way to save Spokane’s daily newspaper, but as part of a growing movement to resurrect dying papers by making them less dependent on ads and corporate ownership and more on philanthropy and community partnerships. As proof of concept, the paper had already added several so-called “community-funded” journalists to its staff. But in the Spokesman-Review newsroom this summer, that hopeful vision ran into persistent concerns about Curley’s leadership. More than a dozen current and former employees, along with contemporaneous records reviewed by InvestigateWest and RANGE, reveal how the newsroom had raised concerns about Curley’s management for years, culminating in his suspension from the paper on Aug. 7 and a vote of no confidence from the union, the Spokane Editorial Society. He is currently on leave as the paper conducts an internal investigation. Employees said stories that might have angered powerful community figures or potential donors were killed or curtailed, and that they felt he retaliated against workers he viewed as disloyal. Staffers questioned his financial oversight of Comma, which hired his own son at a salary topping most reporters’ and recruited out-of-town executives to serve as top editors before Comma had met its fundraising goal. Current and former Spokesman-Review employees also described workplace complaints involving Curley and one of those editors, including allegations of inappropriate lewd and sexual comments around employees, including teenage interns. Curley declined to comment for this article. In a brief phone interview, Curley’s attorney, Patrick Kirby, who specializes in employment and wrongful termination cases, said, “It’s all inaccurate,” in reference to a list of claims InvestigateWest and RANGE provided to Curley prior to publication. Kirby hung up the call when a reporter pressed him on which claims specifically he believed were inaccurate. The top of Page 1 of The Spokesman-Review, April 16, 2025. Tensions in the newsroom came to a head in the first week of August, as the paper rallied to cover the most destructive wildfires in Spokane’s history and the imminent ownership transfer approached at the end of the month. Some staffers were alarmed at the prospect of working for an organization Curley founded, with even fewer checks on his authority. “The terror had been building through advertising, circulation, and this newsroom each day, getting closer to the day of knowing we would have to work for Rob without the filter of human resources and the publisher,” said one employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution. Reporters had grown increasingly frustrated with Comma editors meddling with stories, and Curley tried to fire a reporter who pushed back, employees say. But instead, when other Spokesman-Review editors backed the reporter, publisher William “Stacey” Cowles suspended Curley, citing “ several personnel complaints ” against him. It wasn’t until after Curley’s suspension that reporters were told news that called the Comma plan into question. In a meeting days after Curley had been kicked out of the building, Spokesman-Review management shared that despite public claims by Curley that several reporters were paid for by community donors — a source of optimism for the Comma plan — none of the paper’s reporting positions were currently community-funded. There were “audible gasps,” according to several reporters in the room. The paper had been promoting its community-funded reporters online, removing paywalls for stories written by those journalists. One reporter remembered how at fundraising events, Curley would point to a journalist’s face on a big screen and tell donors that their money paid for journalists’ salaries. Even the reporters took pride in sharing the claim with readers. “I’ve been lying on his behalf without even knowing it,” one reporter said. Cowles, the publisher, said he had no comment on the claims about Curley until the conclusion of the internal investigation. He said the paper is targeting Oct. 30 to close the transaction with Comma. Bill Simer, Comma Community Journalism Lab board chair, did not comment for this article. Saving local journalism Before joining the Spokesman-Review in 2016, Curley had been praised in some journalism circles as a leader in transitioning struggling newspapers away from print and into the digital world. In naming Curley as the Spokesman-Review’s new top editor, Cowles said Curley had “a proven record of delivering news that matters” and that his “innovative work” at previous newspapers helped them win top journalism awards “including a Pulitzer Prize,” the announcement said. But reporters at his previous gigs viewed him differently : as a mercurial leader who hyped expensive, ineffective initiatives, sacrificing journalism ethics to keep up cozy relationships with powerful community institutions and politicians. The Orange County Register in Southern California was criticized for favorable coverage of Disney under Curley, who served as the paper’s top editor between 2014 and 2016 and proudly said he wore a Mickey Mouse garment every day. He also faced backlash when he revised an article two months after it had been published at the request of a politician, despite police reports and other records that didn’t support the change . Curley changed the story over the objections of the reporter and did not note the changes for the public with a correction or editor’s note — a decision journalism ethicists called an “unethical overreach.” Journalists from the Las Vegas Sun in Nevada had their own problems with him. After he left the Sun in 2012, they noticed that Curley kept getting credit for the paper’s Pulitzer Prize in 2009 — credit that Cowles repeated in the 2016 hiring announcement. Sun employees clarified to the Inlander, a Spokane alt-weekly, that Curley, in fact, had nothing to do with the series that won the Pulitzer. Curley said he’d never told anyone he won a Pulitzer, blaming a series of misunderstandings for it showing up time and time again in his biography. Curley stuck around Spokane, undaunted by the controversies from his past. And with layoffs and buyouts shrinking the newsroom in a struggling industry, Curley two years ago began testing the Comma pitch among staff by signaling that it would save their jobs. Reporters said he told them privately that they’d receive big raises once the transfer happened. If Comma didn’t move forward, he said the Cowles family would likely lay off staff or maybe sell the locally owned paper to one of the hedge fund–owned companies known for downsizing newsrooms, one current employee recalled. Reporters felt Curley had compromised editorial independence at the Spokesman as well. Staffers took issue with Curley altering an article in 2025 about a bond proposal from Spokane Public Schools. In the article, reporters wrote a passage explaining how the proposal could raise property taxes. The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.” Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit. Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns. Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself. “That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.” Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024 . The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series. That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors. “We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August. But that’s not what happened. “They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said. The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said. A newsroom altercation As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder. Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment. Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime. Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack. “If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment. In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames. The Review Building, which houses the Spokesman-Review office, in downtown Spokane, Washington on September 30, 2026. (Wilson Criscione/InvestigateWest) On Aug. 4, Sylvester told reporters they should change how they attribute documents in stories. Instead of citing “court documents,” he said they should cite “sworn affidavits.” Despite having no clear editorial role in the Spokesman-Review newsroom, Sylvester went into Duggan’s story that night and made a change reflecting his preference — except in that instance, the record was not in fact an affidavit. It introduced an error into the paper. Clouse, the union president, said he called a meeting with management to try to understand why Comma editors were meddling with stories again. “That never got resolved,” he said. Two days later, Duggan, who’d worked 13 straight days, was finishing up another story about the accused arsonist. Sylvester approached her and said, in a low voice, “you’re doing it again,” several employees who witnessed or learned of the altercation told InvestigateWest and RANGE. He’d been referring to her story saying “court documents.” Duggan walked away. But Sylvester followed, and the two shouted back and forth at each other until other editors stepped in to cool things down. “I wanted to make sure that our stories were truthful and honest and that they were not being edited without us knowing and without any communication,” Duggan said. “And I just wanted to keep the integrity of the paper.” Curley sided with Sylvester, telling Spokesman-Review managing editor Lindsey Treffry that night to fire Duggan. Treffry refused. The next morning, during a series of meetings with Cowles, Treffry and other editors shared complaints they had about Curley. Cowles decided to put Curley on administrative leave, revoking his keycard access to the paper’s offices. A few hours later, however, Curley got in the newsroom again by asking an unsuspecting intern for their keycard. He walked around asking where he could find Treffry, who, according to several staffers there that day, was hiding from Curley in the photo room with other editors. Duggan joined them, and it was there that Duggan learned Treffry saved her job. As they hid, Duggan texted White, who was not in the newsroom at the time. White shared the texts with InvestigateWest and RANGE that described how an HR employee escorted Curley out of the building. “They chased Rob out of the newsroom,” Duggan texted. “I can’t see because I’m hiding.” “I’m hysterical,” Duggan wrote, crumpled into a ball and crying. Duggan said she’d “ride or die for this paper.” She said Curley’s attempt to fire her “felt like a slap in the face — it felt like betrayal.” In an interview for this story, she said she’ll be grateful for the rest of her life that Treffry had her back. “She did save my job. And she protected the rest of us from something similar,” Duggan said. “Jessica Rabbit” Former reporter Rachel Alexander, who worked at the Spokesman-Review from October 2014 to July 2018, recalled a pattern of “cronyism and ethics violations.” In a letter she sent to investigators after Curley’s suspension, Alexander described a departure of women on staff and in leadership roles during Curley’s first year; editors who left meetings with him looking “shaken, exhausted and at times afraid”; and how Curley didn’t keep promises to sponsor a former staff member’s work visa if he left the union. “Despite the meaningful journalism I was able to do and the presence of many talented colleagues who I greatly admire, I could not in good conscience continue working for a man who was willing to lie to a friend and jeopardize his ability to remain in the country,” Alexander wrote. “I made the decision to leave the Spokesman in 2018 primarily because of Mr. Curley’s behavior.” Before leaving, Alexander noticed that she was “nearly the only woman left on the desk,” according to her letter. She also told investigators that Curley seemed to primarily “take issue with or pick fights” with women in the newsroom. Instead of talking through concerns, he made “petty” decisions, like blocking reporters on Twitter, she wrote. In recent years, the paper has hosted high school interns as part of Curley’s effort to make Comma into a training ground for young journalists. But the behavior of Curley and Sylvester made some employees question whether they should be responsible for mentoring young journalists. One letter shared with internal investigators described how, during a 2024 barbecue for Spokesman-Review interns at Curley’s house, two teenage interns saw sexually explicit images of women on Curley’s iPad as he scrolled through his camera roll. Curley had been giving the high school girls a tour of his home and showing off his guitar collection. He was looking for song lyrics on his iPad when the inappropriate pictures flashed on his screen, according to employees who had heard of the incident from the interns. Several staff members also brought concerns to HR about inappropriate comments Sylvester made around interns who were in high school and college. In a conversation with another employee about the evolution of photography — and while sitting near an 18-year-old intern — Sylvester joked that if someone wanted to send a “dick pic” back in the day, they had to wait for it to develop, but today it can be done in an instant. On a different occasion, Sylvester told another employee to wait a few seconds before downloading porn, according to several employees. It was loud enough for other employees to hear the unprompted comment, including nearby interns. “It was very shocking to hear someone … who was supposed to be a mentor figure say that,” a staffer who witnessed the exchange said. “It’s just not appropriate for the workplace.” Current and former staff members also described a work environment where people perceived as being against Curley or who reported issues to HR were retaliated against. They felt Curley had favorites — including Sylvester and Wares — who would not face consequences for their actions. After an employee reported Sylvester to HR for his comment about dick pics, a letter to investigators said Curley appeared to retaliate against those he believed had made the report. Curley excluded one of the employees from important meetings and avoided another employee and gave them “distasteful looks.” Curley needed to make sure staff was “loyal” to him, employees said. They’re not in ours”: USA Today Co. execs defend Palantir deal Link fastcompany.com ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck October 8, 2026 USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir . In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack , three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees . RELATED ARTICLE “An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnership Hanaa' Tameez August 10, 2026 Mike Reed , the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported. In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time: In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project. Lark-Marie Anton , then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools. What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have. In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used . Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal. Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members: Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things. She continued: I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours. Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption. “I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said. Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company , including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff , referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs. “USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.” You can read the full interview on Fast Company.
